title: Permanent Establishment - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Explore the meaning of Permanent Establishment in our Canadian SR&ED glossary and its role in federal and provincial R&D tax credits.
summary: In Canada's SR&ED and provincial R&D tax credit rules, a permanent establishment determines where a corporation can claim. Ontario's OITC, ORDTC and OBRITC all require a permanent establishment in Ontario, and SR&ED contract payments to a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment are excluded from federal qualified expenditures and earn no investment tax credit.

body.text: In Canada's SR&ED and provincial R&D tax credit rules, a permanent establishment determines where a corporation can claim. Ontario's OITC, ORDTC and OBRITC all require a permanent establishment in Ontario, and SR&ED contract payments to a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment are excluded from federal qualified expenditures and earn no investment tax credit.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive landscape has undergone its most substantial structural expansion in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program provides an enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures—doubling the previous $3,000,000 baseline limit and raising the maximum annual enhanced credit to $2,100,000. Simultaneously, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) have expanded from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to a broader $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range. For the first time, access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC has been extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), a mechanism into which CCPCs may also elect. Furthermore, Parliament has restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, alongside equipment lease expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), while launching an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) on April 1, 2026.

At the sub-national level, provincial and territorial alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms has diverged sharply across jurisdictions. British Columbia expressly harmonized its 10% SR&ED tax credit with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out range, ECPC refundability, and capital expenditure restoration, while BC Budget 2026 permanently eliminated the provincial credit's sunset clause. Quebec overhauled its innovation tax architecture for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing four legacy R&D credits with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which delivers a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess. Conversely, Ontario (8% refundable OITC capped at $3,000,000; 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC; 20% refundable OBRITC) and Alberta (8% base and 20% incremental Innovation Employment Grant capped at $4,000,000 on current expenditures) have retained their independent expenditure caps and phase-out parameters, with Alberta also continuing to exclude capital expenditures.
1. Statutory and Legislative Framework of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Architecture under the Income Tax Act

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is a statutory entitlement administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which oversees technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and tax return processing—and the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy. Unlike discretionary government grants that are subject to fixed budgetary envelopes, any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs eligible SR&ED work in Canada and satisfies the statutory filing deadlines is legally entitled to claim SR&ED tax incentives under the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act") and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations").

Computing an SR&ED claim requires executing two legally related but mathematically distinct statutory calculations under the Act. The first calculation determines the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37. Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may accumulate allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada in a cumulative expenditure pool. Specifically, paragraph 37(1)(a) governs expenditures of a current nature, including the directly engaged portion of employee salaries and wages, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), third-party payments to Canadian-resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), third-party payments to approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, and granting councils under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii), third-party payments to tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and directly attributable overhead expenditures when the traditional method is elected. Following the enactment of Bill C-15, paragraph 37(1)(b) once again includes expenditures of a capital nature incurred for depreciable property acquired and available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024. Amounts in the Section 37 pool may be deducted in full or in part to reduce net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

The second calculation determines Qualified SR&ED Expenditures and Investment Tax Credits under Sections 127 and 127.1. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Where the claimant is entitled to a cash refund of unused ITCs after reducing Part I federal tax payable, section 127.1 (subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(3)) governs the calculation and deemed deduction of the "refundable investment tax credit".

A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that "allowable SR&ED expenditure" (under Section 37) and "qualified expenditure" (under Subsection 127(9)) are not interchangeable terms. Several statutory adjustments create divergences between the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC base. First, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under the proxy method (Regulation 2900(4)) is a notional overhead amount added solely to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool to generate ITCs; it is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Second, payments made to arm's length subcontractors for SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf and third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool, but are restricted to 80% inclusion in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Third, payments under SR&ED contracts to non-arm's length (NAL) performers are deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool, but are strictly excluded from the payer's Section 127 qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(24) unless the performer's underlying qualified expenditures are formally transferred via Form T1146 pursuant to subsection 127(13). Fourth, expenditures on used depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 (reported on Line 390 of Form T661) enter the Section 37 deduction pool, but do not qualify for the Section 127 ITC unless vendor refurbishments meet the CRA's strict "new state" standard. Fifth, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024 is depreciated under normal Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8 rather than entering the Section 37 pool, yet 25% of its capital cost in each of two qualifying periods is added to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool on Line 504 of Form T661.

Under subsection 37(1.1) of the Act, when a corporate claimant performs SR&ED that relates to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a parent or sister company, determined without reference to control by right), the SR&ED is considered to relate to a business of the claimant at the time the expenditure or payment is made, provided the related corporation is actively engaged in that business at that time. In addition, subsection 37(1.3) addresses SR&ED performed in Canada's exclusive economic zone. While current expenditures for R&D conducted outside Canada may be deducted as ordinary current business expenses under subsection 37(2), they cannot be claimed on Form T661 and earn no ITCs—with the sole exception of permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada, which are subject to the statutory limit determined under subsection 37(1.5). Finally, subsection 37(4) prohibits any deduction or ITC for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing existing patents or intellectual property), preventing duplication of tax incentives between the performer and a subsequent purchaser.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Prior to 1996, the legislative definition of scientific research and experimental development resided in Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. In 1996, Parliament added the definition directly to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, where it continues to govern all federal and harmonized provincial R&D claims.

Pursuant to subsection 248(1) of the Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of three primary categories of core work, supplemented by one category of eligible support work and bounded by seven statutory exclusions.

The three core categories of eligible SR&ED work are set out in paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), and (c). Paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research investigates underlying natural phenomena, physical laws, or theoretical structures solely to expand the scientific knowledge base. Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Like basic research, applied research is often conducted in a laboratory setting and seeks to generate new scientific knowledge, but directs that inquiry toward a defined practical objective—such as efforts to develop a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that virus. Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development) encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada. Crucially, the statute explicitly covers incremental improvements to existing materials, devices, products, or processes, provided those improvements seek technological advancement through resolving technological uncertainty rather than applying routine engineering.

In applying the definition of SR&ED in respect of a taxpayer, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight strictly enumerated categories:

items: Engineering (the practice of designing, composing, evaluating, advising, reporting, directing, or supervising construction or manufacturing that requires engineering science);
Design (work to transform concepts and ideas into a plan);
Operations research;
Mathematical analysis (the examination of a set of observations by means of mathematical tools, principles, methods, or techniques);
Computer programming (preparing and coding operating instructions for a computer);
Data collection (gathering information using pre-determined procedures);
Testing; and
Psychological research (research into the functions of the mind and behaviour of humans or animals, such as human-machine interaction, when supporting non-social science/humanities SR&ED).

body.text: Under paragraph 248(1)(d), work within these eight categories does not constitute SR&ED on its own. Rather, support work is eligible if and only if its extent is "commensurate with the needs" (corresponding in amount, size, extent, or duration to what is necessary) and "directly in support of" basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Conversely, the concluding portion of the definition in subsection 248(1) expressly excludes any work carried out with respect to seven enumerated activities in paragraphs (e) to (k):

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion (including examining buying habits, use of leisure time, consumer needs or wants, attitudes toward existing or test-marketed products, market development, market verification, market demonstration, customer acceptance, and sales promotion);
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; or
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection (gathering information that supports normal business operations).

body.text: As the CRA emphasizes in its administrative guidelines, distinguishing between eligible paragraph (d) support work (such as data collection or testing) and ineligible paragraphs (f) and (k) excluded work (such as routine testing or routine data collection) turns on the purpose for which the activity was performed. If testing or data collection is carried out specifically to perform and directly support the scientific research or experimental development work, it qualifies as support work under paragraph (d); if it is performed for normal business operations or commercial quality verification, it is excluded.
1.3 CRA Eligibility Methodology: From the Five Questions to the Why and How Requirements

Historically, the CRA administered work eligibility under its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (dated April 24, 2015), which structured the eligibility evaluation around a Two-Step Methodology incorporating Five Questions derived directly from the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998). In Step 1 (Determine if there is SR&ED), the CRA examined the details of the work to determine whether five sequential questions could be answered in the affirmative: (1) Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?. Once Step 1 confirmed the existence of eligible SR&ED, Step 2 (Determine the extent of eligible work) established the boundaries of the project by including commensurate paragraph (d) support work and excluding paragraphs (e) to (k) excluded work.

On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy document and its five-question framing with the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines consolidate the statutory analysis into two overarching requirements that must both be met for work to qualify as SR&ED: why the work is conducted and how the work is conducted.

Under the "Why" Requirement, work must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving an advancement of scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or a technological advancement (experimental development). Generating new scientific or technological knowledge requires encountering a scientific or technological uncertainty—a limitation or gap in the existing "scientific or technological knowledge base" (defined as the combined knowledge of the qualified resources within the business plus all sources that are reasonably available publicly) that cannot be resolved through standard practice or routine engineering. Crucially, achieving commercial novelty, innovation, uniqueness, feature enhancement, or increased functionality of a product or process does not in itself demonstrate scientific or technological advancement; conversely, a project does not have to achieve a commercially successful outcome to qualify, as determining through experiment that a technological uncertainty cannot be resolved still generates new technological knowledge.

Under the "How" Requirement, the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA Guidelines specify that this systematic approach includes four core elements: (1) generating an idea (hypothesis) consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem or uncertainty; (2) testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. Furthermore, the CRA defines the completion date of an SR&ED project—the point at which work eligibility ceases—as the earliest point at which the claimant achieved the scientific or technological advancement by resolving the associated uncertainties, determined that the uncertainties cannot be resolved, or terminated the project for any reason.
2. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Carryovers
2.1 Enactment of the 2025–2026 Legislative Enhancements (Bill C-15)

The current financial parameters of the federal SR&ED program reflect a two-stage legislative expansion initiated in late 2024 and enacted into law in March 2026. In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) released in December 2024, the Department of Finance initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, increasing the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and reintroducing the eligibility of capital expenditures for property acquired after December 15, 2024. Subsequently, Budget 2025 proposed further increasing the annual enhanced expenditure limit from the previously announced $4,500,000 to $6,000,000.

Parliament enacted these consolidated Budget 2025 SR&ED reforms into law through Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. All core rate, threshold, ECPC, and capital expenditure provisions in Bill C-15 apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (meaning a calendar-year corporation accesses the new rules starting with its January 1, 2025 taxation year).

Alongside the SR&ED enhancements, Bill C-15 enacted the Productivity Super-Deduction, a set of enhanced tax incentives covering new capital investments that allows businesses to write off a larger share of the cost of capital investments immediately. On September 15, 2026, the Department of Finance released draft legislative proposals for a separate Productivity Mega Deduction, which would permanently extend immediate expensing to a broad range of depreciable property acquired on or after September 15, 2026; this measure is a proposal and has not been enacted. This operates alongside the enhanced 100% first-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) deduction for Class 44, Class 46, and Class 50 (electronic data processing equipment and systems software, otherwise depreciable at 55% declining balance) for eligible property acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027, as well as Class 12 application software (100% depreciable over two years at 50% in Year 1 and 50% in Year 2). Where a taxpayer claims an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, the taxpayer must not include that same expenditure on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance (CCA)), ensuring no double-dipping between SR&ED capital pooling and regular CCA.
2.2 Claimant Categories, Credit Rates, and Refundability Mechanics

Under subsection 127(9) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, both the ITC rate (35% enhanced vs. 15% basic) and the refundability rate (the percentage of unused current-year ITC remaining after offsetting Part I federal income tax payable that may be refunded in cash) depend on the legal category of the claimant and whether the expenditure is of a current or capital nature.

The basic federal SR&ED ITC rate under subsection 127(9) is 15% (reduced from 20% for taxation years ending after 2013), calculated as 15% of the excess of the claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts. It applies to corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate, to qualified expenditures incurred by CCPCs or ECPCs above their annual expenditure limit, and to unincorporated individuals (sole proprietors), partnerships, and trusts. Under subsection 127(10.1), qualifying CCPCs and (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an additional 20% enhancement on top of the 15% basic rate—yielding an enhanced 35% ITC rate—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit (maximum $6,000,000).

For Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), refundability depends on whether the CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" or an "excluded corporation" as defined in subsection 127.1(2) of the Act. A "qualifying corporation" is a CCPC throughout the taxation year whose taxable income in the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable income of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year, calculated before specified future tax consequences) does not exceed its qualifying income limit. A qualifying CCPC (that is not an excluded corporation) receives 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures (and PPA) up to the expenditure limit, 40% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and 40% refundability on its 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the expenditure limit. If a CCPC is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation (because its prior-year taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit), it still receives 100% refundability on the 35% enhanced ITC for current expenditures (and 40% for capital expenditures) within its expenditure limit, but receives 0% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned above the limit. Conversely, a CCPC that is an "excluded corporation" is restricted to 40% refundability on both current and capital expenditures within the limit and 40% refundability on expenditures above the limit.

An Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is defined in subsection 127(9) as a corporation that is resident in Canada, is a public corporation (listed on a designated stock exchange) or a 90%-owned subsidiary of such a corporation, and is not controlled by non-residents. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC earns the 35% enhanced ITC up to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, with 100% refundability on current expenditures (and PPA) and 40% refundability on capital expenditures within the limit. Any expenditures incurred by an ECPC above its expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC, which is non-refundable (0%).

For partnerships (subsection 96(1) and subsection 127(8)), a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 deductible expenditure pool to a subsequent year; under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), the partnership's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income in the year incurred. Furthermore, a partnership does not itself claim an ITC; under subsection 127(8), the credit is calculated at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate and allocated to eligible partners. Qualifying corporate partners, individuals, and certain trusts may receive a 40% refund on their allocated 15% partnership ITC, whereas corporate partners that are not qualifying corporations cannot receive a cash refund.

A. CCPC Expenditure Limit Formula (Subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.4))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC that does not elect into the revenue method determines its annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and any associated corporations under subsection 127(10.21)) for its immediately preceding taxation year:

In this formula, variable A is nil ($0) if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and in any other case is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. Consequently, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit drops by $100,000 for every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. (Practitioners should note that the SR&ED taxable capital phase-out of $15,000,000–$75,000,000 no longer lines up with the $10,000,000–$50,000,000 taxable capital grind on the federal small business deduction, requiring separate calculations for growing associated corporate groups). For taxation years shorter than 51 weeks, the expenditure limit is prorated by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365 (for example, 273 days out of 365 yields an expenditure limit of $4,487,671). Where CCPCs are associated, the single group expenditure limit must be allocated among the associated members via Schedule T2SCH49 under subsection 127(10.3); failure to file an agreement triggers subsection 127(10.4), while subsection 127(10.5) governs expenditure limit determinations in special cases.

body.text: 2.4 Pool Deductions, Carrybacks, Carryforwards, and Taxability of ITCs

Deductions from the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures are optional in any given taxation year (except for partnerships), allowing a claimant to deduct any amount up to the available pool balance or carry the unclaimed balance forward indefinitely to future taxation years. If the claimant is a corporation or trust and experiences a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control), subsection 37(6.1) restricts the deductibility of the undeducted pool balance: the pre-acquisition pool may only be deducted when the business to which the expenditures related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent that the claimant's income for the taxation year (before making any Section 37 deduction) is derived from that same business or a similar business. On an amalgamation or wind-up, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures transfers to the continuing corporation.

For the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit, any unused non-refundable ITC (such as the remaining $90,000 in the worked example above) that is not deducted against federal Part I tax in the current year or refunded in cash may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable. A carryback to a prior year is limited to the lesser of: (1) the portion of the current-year ITC not deductible in the current year, and (2) the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in the previous taxation year exceeds the ITC available in that previous year (taking into account any ITC refunded in that previous year). Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax in the year, reducing the ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward. Where an acquisition of control occurs, special statutory rules restrict how unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control can be carried forward and how unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control can be carried back.

Finally, federal SR&ED ITCs that are deducted from Part I tax under subsection 127(5) or refunded under section 127.1 in a given taxation year (Year 1) are taxed in the following taxation year (Year 2). Specifically, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Act, the amount of any federal SR&ED ITC applied or refunded in the preceding taxation year (including ITCs relating to the Prescribed Proxy Amount, other than an ITC allocated from a partnership) reduces the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in Year 2. If those reductions cause the Section 37 pool balance to become negative at the end of Year 2, the negative amount must be included in the taxpayer's taxable income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the Act, and an equivalent amount is subsequently added back to the Section 37 pool in the next taxation year.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

When preparing Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), a claimant must elect between two statutory calculation methods for overhead and other expenditures. Under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)), the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates all qualifying SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (Regulation 2900(2)(c)) or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED (Regulation 2900(3)). Under the Traditional Method, itemized overhead enters both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. If a claimant does not select a calculation method on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method by default.

Conversely, under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and Regulation 2900(4)), the claimant does not track or include any SR&ED overhead and other expenditures in its SR&ED claim. Instead, in Part 5 of Form T661, the claimant calculates a notional amount called the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. (Since 2014, the prescribed proxy rate has been 55%, following historical rates of 60% for 2013 and 65% for 2012 and earlier years). Under the Proxy Method, the actual business overhead expenses represented by the PPA remain ordinary business expenses deductible in calculating net income under Section 9 of the Act, while the notional 55% PPA is added only to the Section 127 qualified expenditure calculation to earn ITCs (and is never added to the Section 37 deductible pool). The PPA is also subject to an overall PPA cap ensuring that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specific allowable deductions under the Regulations do not exceed the total business expenditures made by the claimant in the year. The choice between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method is made on a year-by-year basis, and once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that year.
3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the Proxy Salary Base
A. General Eligibility and the "Directly Engaged" Test

Under subsection 248(1) of the Act, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act. It includes basic salary or wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements, non-competition payments, and qualifying taxable benefits (provided non-cash benefits represent a reasonable estimate of actual cost incurred and are not claimed under Section 9). Where a taxable benefit included on an employee's T4 slip contains a GST/HST or PST component for which the employer can claim an input tax credit (or provincial credit), subsection 248(16) deems that input tax credit to be government assistance; therefore, no GST/HST or PST amount may be included in allowable SR&ED salary or wages. Conversely, dividends paid to shareholder-employees, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, extended vacation or sick leave, and the employer's share of related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or EHT contributions) are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages. Furthermore, under subsection 78(4) of the Act, any employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and is only claimable in the subsequent year when paid (reported on Line 310 of Form T661).

To be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages, the employee must be "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada. As set out in the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "directly engaged" refers to hands-on work, determined as a question of fact based on the actual tasks performed rather than the employee's job title ("directly" meaning proceeding from one point to another without deviation, interruption, or an intervening step or intermediary). Work performed by non-specialized employees can qualify as "directly engaged" under the proxy method only if: (1) the work is directly in support of, and forms an integral part of, basic or applied research or experimental development (such as operating a machine specifically for an experiment, feeding raw materials for an experiment, or performing welding, machining, electrical, or plumbing work that is an integral part of an SR&ED project), and (2) the work is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Equipment maintenance or repairs, materials handling, and clerical or administrative support activities do not qualify as directly engaged under the proxy method. Under the Traditional Method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) and Regulation 2900(2)(b)), employee remuneration may be claimed on a directly attributable basis or at 100% if the employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their time on SR&ED.
B. Restrictions on Specified Employees (Subsections 37(9), 37(9.1), 37(9.3), and Regulation 2900(4))

A "specified employee" is defined under subsection 248(1) of the Act with reference to the non-arm's length rules in section 251 as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder (for example, a controlling or sole shareholder or a related family member). The Act imposes four strict statutory limitations on specified employees:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): While bonuses and remuneration based on profits are allowable in the Section 37 pool for non-specified employees (though excluded from the Proxy Salary Base), subsection 37(9) strictly prohibits claiming any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee.

Section 37 Deductible Pool Cap (Subsection 37(9.1) — 5 × YMPE): Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) and subsection 37(9.1), the maximum claimable SR&ED expenditure for salary or wages of a specified employee is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), prorated for the number of days the person was a specified employee during the year.

Proxy Salary Base Cap (Regulation 2900(4) — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE): For purposes of calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661, the amount of a specified employee's salary or wages included in the Salary Base is restricted to the lesser of: (i) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED wages, but excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year), or (ii) 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the year.

Associated Corporations Allocation (Subsection 37(9.3) and Form T1174): A specified employee working for two or more associated corporations cannot have their SR&ED salary claimed unless the corporations file an agreement using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) under subsection 37(9.3). Similarly, the total salary or wages included in the Proxy Salary Base for a specified employee across all associated corporations (including related individuals and partnerships with related/associated partners) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year cannot exceed 2.5 times the YMPE and must be shared between them.

body.text: 3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) and Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may include the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

As codified in the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" refers to all the raw materials, substances, or other items that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process. The raw materials, substances, or other items must be physical and tangible (generally in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state), and the "thing" must be a tangible object (an intermediate product, a by-product, or a final product) on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED being carried out (or, for new or improved processes, a tangible object involved in testing the process).
Materials are classified into two categories:

items: Materials Consumed: Materials that are destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or used up in the prosecution of SR&ED. Examples include cardboard boxes used to test a new printing process that have no residual value after testing and are disposed of as waste, or animal feed, plant fertilizer, pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides used on animals or plants involved in SR&ED (provided the SR&ED is not conducted simultaneously with commercial production). Materials consumed are claimable only in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Materials Transformed: Materials that are changed or incorporated into another tangible object as a result of SR&ED, but are not completely consumed or rendered virtually valueless (retaining some value). Examples include materials incorporated into a custom product or commercial asset (such as an experimental engine incorporated into a commercial machine), input materials forming part of experimental production resulting from experimental development (ED+EP, such as yarn converted into fabric during an experimental production run), or component parts used in testing that retain value. While materials transformed are claimable in the taxation year of transformation, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) trigger ITC recapture if the transformed materials (or biological assets such as animals or growing things, excluding control groups on which no SR&ED is performed) are later sold or converted to commercial use.

body.text: Items that do not compose the physical body of a thing on which SR&ED is performed are not materials for SR&ED (unless they are themselves the subject of the SR&ED), though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method. Specifically excluded from SR&ED materials are: cleaning products; discs, CDs, or DVDs used in computers; test tubes, pipettes, vials, bottles, beakers, flasks, dishes, and other glass or plastic labware; microscopes, incubators, Bunsen burners, and measuring appliances; filter papers; acids, solvents, lubricants (such as engine oil), and soaps used in processing; and general utilities such as water, electricity, oil, and natural gas (unless water is directly consumed as part of the SR&ED and its portion is clearly documented and verified). Materials can be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers as long as they are used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. However, if materials are purchased from a non-arm's length (NAL) person or partnership, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the ITC to the "adjusted selling cost" incurred by the NAL party, excluding any inter-company profit element.
3.4 Subcontractor Expenditures and Third-Party Payments
A. Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Subsection 127(9))

Where a claimant (the payer) contracts with an arm's length party (the performer) to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) or (B)(II)), 100% of the current contract expenditure is an allowable SR&ED expenditure in the Section 37 pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), whereas only 80% of the expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 ITC calculation under subsection 127(9). To earn an ITC on an arm's length contract, the payer must demonstrate that the SR&ED was carried on in Canada by a "taxable supplier" (if a contract is paid or payable to a non-taxable supplier, such as a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment, it is excluded from qualified expenditures) and that the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant. Where a single contract combines SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, only the portion reasonably allocated to the SR&ED work carried out in Canada qualifies.

For the arm's length contractor (performer), if it carries out basic research, applied research, or experimental development on behalf of a Canadian payer, the contractor can claim its own SR&ED expenditures, but must reduce its qualified expenditures by any contract payments received or receivable (subsection 127(9)). Furthermore, under the look-through rule in subsections 37(14) and 37(15), a payer's SR&ED contract expenditure must be reduced by any related expenditure of the performer that is not of a current nature (such as capital expenditures made prior to December 16, 2024, for which the performer must notify the payer in writing without delay if requested or within 90 days after calendar year-end); for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, capital expenditure eligibility has been restored.
B. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Subsections 37(13), 127(13), and 127(24))

When a claimant awards an SR&ED contract to a non-arm's length (NAL) party (section 251), special statutory rules apply under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy. First, while the contract expenditure is an allowable Section 37 deduction for the NAL payer, subsection 127(24) excludes the payment from being a qualified expenditure for calculating the payer's ITC. Second, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures at cost (eliminating inter-company profit via adjusted service cost), and amounts received or receivable under NAL contracts are not considered "contract payments" and therefore do not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures. Third, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or a portion of the NAL performer's qualified expenditures to the NAL payer (up to the contract amount, reported on Line 540 of Form T661 by the performer).

Fourth, with respect to support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)), while an arm's length performer contracted only for support work cannot claim SR&ED (though the payer can claim 80% of the contract cost), subsection 37(13) (the linking rule) deems support work performed by a non-arm's length performer to be SR&ED provided the work would be SR&ED if performed directly by the payer—allowing the NAL performer to claim the support work expenditures and either keep the ITC or transfer the qualified expenditures via Form T1146. Finally, under subsection 127(24), a claimant cannot circumvent NAL contract rules by inserting an arm's length intermediary between a payer and a NAL performer; if the main purpose of the arrangement is to obtain a qualified expenditure for the payment to the arm's length party, the payer's qualified expenditure is disallowed while the payments received retain their character as contract payments, resulting in none of the entities being entitled to claim an ITC.
C. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), (iii) and Form T1263)

As detailed in the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a third-party payment is a payment in money or in kind made to a qualifying external organization to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada that relates to a business of the claimant, where the third party controls the research and the claimant holds non-exclusive rights but is entitled to exploit the results. Only 80% of a qualifying third-party payment qualifies for an ITC. Claimants must complete and attach a separate Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) for each third-party payment. The Act establishes six recipient entity categories (Entities A through F):

items: Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)): A corporation resident in Canada (eligible on an accrual basis in the year the SR&ED is performed).
Entity B (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): An approved association (eligible on a cash basis in the year paid, exempted from prepaid expense limits under paragraph 18(9)(d)).

Entity C (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): An approved university, college, research institute, or other similar institution (universities and affiliated colleges are inherently approved; eligible on a cash basis when paid).
Entity D (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): A non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j).

Entity E (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)): An approved organization (granting council)—such as the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC), or the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC)—that makes payments to an association, institution, or corporation identified as a B, C, or D entity.

Entity F (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)): A non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada, exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j), for basic or applied research carried on in Canada whose primary purpose is for the corporate claimant to use the results in conjunction with its own SR&ED.

body.text: To satisfy the "entitlement to exploit the results" requirement, if the SR&ED results in a product or patent, the claimant must have the right to use the resulting patent (even for a royalty) or be entitled to distribute or market the resulting product; if the SR&ED results in a gain of general knowledge (such as a scientific paper), the claimant must be granted a preferential right as a direct consequence of the payment, such as access to unpublished results or a prepublication print prior to public domain release. Moreover, the specific taxpayer making the payment must hold the entitlement to exploit (for example, an individual shareholder making a payment personally does not qualify if only their corporation is entitled to exploit the results).

body.text: 3.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Prescribed Expenditures
A. Traditional Method Overhead (Regulation 2900(2)(c) and Regulation 2900(3))

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, it may claim SR&ED overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 under two regulatory provisions as set out in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. First, under Regulation 2900(2)(c), other expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualify if and only if they satisfy both the "directly related" test (there must be a direct linkage with no intervening step or intermediary between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED) and the "incremental" test (the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred). Second, under Regulation 2900(3)(a) and (b), expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada include the prorated cost of maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment (based on actual SR&ED usage rather than fixed-cost maintenance contracts), plus other incremental expenditures directly related to that provision.
Under these tests, the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy establishes specific rules for individual expense items under the Traditional Method:

items: Clerical/Administrative Staff, Non-SR&ED Contracts, & Employer Benefits (Sections 4.1–4.3): The portion of salaries and employer-paid related benefits for clerical and administrative staff providing a service directly to SR&ED employees, non-SR&ED contract costs (such as electricians, welders, or mechanics) that are directly related and incremental, and the employer's share of related benefits for SR&ED staff qualify on Line 360.

Retiring Allowances (Section 4.4): A retiring allowance paid to compensate for a loss of employment qualifies under the Traditional Method if it is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED, allocated based on the employee's historical SR&ED salary ratio and years of service.

Recruitment and Relocation Costs (Section 4.5): Headhunter fees, job advertising expenses, selection travel costs, and immigration/work permit/visa costs are ineligible as SR&ED overhead (deductible only as ordinary business expenses). Conversely, moving expenses (subsection 62(3)) related to relocating selected candidates or existing SR&ED employees to a facility within Canada, as well as taxable employee housing-loss benefits (subsections 6(19) and 6(20)), qualify in both the Section 37 pool and for ITCs if directly related and incremental.

Telecommunications, Travel, Training, and Clinical Studies (Section 4.7): Fixed monthly telephone, cellular, and internet costs fail the incremental test and are ineligible (only identifiable long-distance charges directly related and incremental to SR&ED qualify). Travel and lodging in Canada to perform testing at a customer location, training costs in Canada, incremental utilities, periodical subscriptions, health and safety expenses, and fees paid to clinical study volunteers may qualify under the Traditional Method. Waste disposal costs incurred after the SR&ED activity that produced the scrap has finished are ineligible.

body.text: B. Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and Software Licences

The treatment of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud) and software licences depends on the calculation method elected. Under the Proxy Method, cloud and CAD software subscriptions are not eligible as separate SR&ED expenditures because they are neither T4 salaries, tangible physical materials, nor SR&ED contracts; instead, they are represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. However, computers and software purchased outright after December 15, 2024 and used all or substantially all (≥90%) for SR&ED in Canada qualify as restored SR&ED capital expenditures (or Shared-Use Equipment if new and used >50% to <90%). Under the Traditional Method, cloud infrastructure costs incurred specifically for development and experimental testing environments (segregated from production hosting costs and staging/QA costs) can be claimed as directly attributable overhead on Line 360. For financial accounting vs. tax alignment, while ASPE (Section 3064) and IFRS (IAS 38) require capitalizing software development phase costs once technical and commercial feasibility criteria are met, tax rules allow eligible SR&ED software expenditures to be pooled under Section 37 (subject to subsection 18(9) prepaid expense limits for services extending beyond 365 days), while non-SR&ED commercial application software falls under CCA Class 12 (50% per year over 2 years) and systems software/hardware falls under Class 50 (55% declining balance or 100% first-year enhanced deduction before 2027).
C. Prescribed Expenditures (Regulation 2902)

Under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, certain "prescribed expenditures" are strictly excluded from being qualified expenditures for ITC purposes—even if they are directly related and incremental to SR&ED under the Traditional Method:

items: General administration or management of a business (subparagraph 2902(a)(i)), except for specific directly attributable salary or wages (clause 2902(a)(i)(A));
Legal or accounting fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B));
Interest and other financing costs (clause 2902(a)(i)(C) and paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g));
Entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses, membership dues, and fines or penalties;
Costs to attend conventions or conferences (clause 2902(a)(i)(F)), even if technical and specific to the SR&ED project; and
Fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims.

body.text: 3.6 Capital Expenditures, Equipment Leases, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, and equipment lease costs were excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Following the enactment of Bill C-15, updated CRA policies—the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), and the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026)—govern the restored regime for property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III))

To claim an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 (and report the 10 most expensive properties per project on Lines 262/263 and Box 782 of Form T661), the expenditure must result in the acquisition of depreciable property (subsection 13(21)) owned by the claimant that was both acquired after December 15, 2024 and became available for use after December 15, 2024 (subsections 37(1.2), 127(11.2), and 13(27)). Furthermore, the property must satisfy the All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) Intent Test at the time of acquisition: the claimant must intend that the property will either (1) be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or (2) have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Because the intent test is evaluated over the entire expected useful life of the asset, property acquired for both SR&ED and commercial use normally fails the ASA capital test.

Under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e), non-depreciable property (such as land, inventory, or goodwill), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures (with an exception for prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903). Under the Proxy Method, expenditures for general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) are also excluded. Expenditures on used depreciable equipment entered on Line 390 enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but do not qualify for the Section 127 ITC unless vendor refurbishments prior to acquisition replaced or rebuilt major parts to such an extent that the equipment was brought to a "new state" equivalent to newly manufactured equipment (refurbishments made by the claimant after December 15, 2024 to its own existing SR&ED equipment also qualify). Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are treated as deemed capital cost allowance and must never be included on Schedule T2SCH8. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on qualifying capital expenditures is 40% refundable.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11))

Where new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 does not meet the ≥90% ASA intent test, but is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) reported on Line 504 (and Part 6C / Box 792 for the 20 most expensive SUE expenditures) of Form T661. To qualify, SUE must be new (unused and unrented prior to acquisition), cannot be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and cannot be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, equipment intended for assembling/commissioning a commercial manufacturing plant or line under paragraph 2900(11)(c), or property intended primarily for non-SR&ED over its expected useful life under paragraph 2900(11)(d)).

The full capital cost of SUE is not included in the Section 37 deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the equipment under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8. For Section 127 ITC purposes (identical under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods), the qualified expenditure on Line 504 is 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the equipment (excluding borrowed money interest under section 21 and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) for first term shared-use-equipment (where the equipment is used >50% for SR&ED during the first period, beginning when available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year occurring at least 12 months after that time) and an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost for second term shared-use-equipment (where the equipment qualified as first-term SUE and is used >50% for SR&ED during the second period, beginning when available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time)—allowing up to 50% of the SUE capital cost to earn an ITC across the two periods.
C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)-(II), (B)(I), and (B)(VI))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (excluding building rent under subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i) unless a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903) qualify as current SR&ED expenditures. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of the time for SR&ED in the taxation year, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure; if used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, a proportional share of the lease cost (matching the percentage of SR&ED time) may be claimed on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure if directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method (which excludes GPOEF and land leases), if leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost may be claimed; if used more than 50% to less than 90% ("Primarily") of its operating time for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the lease cost may be claimed; and if used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed.
