body.text: 3.7 Pilot Plants, Prototypes, Commercial Assets, Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP), and ITC Recapture
A. Developing Assets During SR&ED (SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy)
When SR&ED in a commercial environment involves the design, construction, and testing of an asset, the CRA classifies the asset into one of four categories:

items: Pilot Plant: A non-commercial-scale production facility isolated from commercial operations and developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED over its entire useful life (generating experimental production, ED+EP). Labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving technological uncertainties to construct and operate a true pilot plant qualify as current SR&ED expenditures (whereas facilities intended to be converted to commercial operations during or after SR&ED are not pilot plants).

Prototype: An original trial model or preliminary version possessing the essential characteristics of the intended product, built to test technical feasibility within a systematic investigation and generally having no lasting value. Design, construction, and testing costs of a prototype are eligible current expenditures. Duplicate copies constructed for commercial inventory are ineligible, whereas duplicate copies built strictly for testing that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of SR&ED qualify as materials consumed or transformed when testing concludes.

Commercial Plant, Custom Product, or Commercial Asset: A commercial plant or commercial asset is developed for internal use in the company's own business, whereas a custom product is developed for sale to meet specific customer requirements. Claimants must segregate SR&ED work from non-SR&ED commercial work and claim only the labour, materials consumed, and materials transformed in resolving technological uncertainties (subject to ITC recapture on transformed materials upon sale or commercial conversion).

The Alternative Approach for Custom Products / Commercial Assets: In cases where it is very difficult to apportion expenses between SR&ED and commercial work, the CRA accepts an Alternative Approach (available under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods, but not for years subsequent to the first CRA review where the claimant used this approach, and subject to CRA agreement on the estimation basis). Under this formula, allowable SR&ED expenditures equal the total actual costs of developing the asset minus the estimated costs that would usually be associated with constructing the asset if the technology had already existed, plus the cost of materials transformed in SR&ED. For example, if a claimant incurs $150,000 in total project costs to develop a machine with an improved engine, estimates that the machine would cost $125,000 if the technology had already existed, and estimates $30,000 of materials transformed in the improved engine, the allowable SR&ED expenditure is ($150,000 − $125,000) + $30,000 = $55,000 (with the $30,000 of transformed materials subject to ITC recapture).

body.text: B. SR&ED During Production Runs: ED+EP vs. ED+CP (SR&ED During Production Runs Policy)
When experimental development occurs during an industrial production run, the CRA evaluates each production run individually to determine its "context":

items: ED+EP (Experimental Development Resulting in Experimental Production): Applies when there is no simultaneous commercial work and there is technical risk to the process or product attributable to technological uncertainties—such as testing process parameters outside normal established ranges where there is a risk of process instability, output inconsistencies, stoppages, yield losses above normal, or equipment damage. In an ED+EP run, directly engaged salaries, materials consumed, materials transformed into the experimental production required to evaluate the SR&ED (excluding any excess production beyond what is required for SR&ED), and incremental Traditional Method overhead are allowable SR&ED expenditures (subject to ITC recapture on transformed materials if the experimental output is sold or converted to commercial use).

ED+CP (Experimental Development in Conjunction or Simultaneously with Commercial Production): Applies when SR&ED is carried out simultaneously with commercial production in an existing facility while monitoring indicators to avoid adverse effects on product quality or process stability (no technical risk to the commercial product or process). In an ED+CP run, all costs usually incurred for normal commercial production must be excluded; only the additional (incremental) labour, incremental material losses (actual material losses minus standard processing losses), and incremental overhead associated with the experimental development are allowable. Where neither the claimant nor the CRA can isolate the SR&ED work in an ED+CP run, they may agree to use the Incremental Cost Method (Actual costs incurred for the ED+CP run minus Standard production costs for commercial production without ED), provided the claimant signs a formal waiver of its right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the Act.

body.text: C. Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

As codified in subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a claimant must report an SR&ED ITC recapture (adding the recaptured amount to Part I tax payable) when all four conditions are met simultaneously:

items: The claimant acquired a particular tangible property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(36));

The cost of the property (or a portion thereof) was a qualified expenditure (such as materials transformed, capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment [SUE], or SR&ED contracts resulting in the acquisition of tangible property);
A percentage of that property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and
In the taxation year, the claimant either converts to commercial use or disposes of the particular property (or another property that incorporates the particular property).

body.text: Under subsection 127(32), the "cost" of property for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire a property from another person; it never includes internal salaries, wages, or overhead costs imputed to manufacturing a component in-house (whereas ordering an experimental part from an arm's length supplier for $12,000 subjects the full $12,000 to recapture). Furthermore, recapture never applies to the sale or licensing of Intellectual Property (IP) where IP accrued to the payer under an SR&ED contract, nor does it apply under the 10% de minimis scrap rule where proceeds of disposition (or Fair Market Value [FMV] upon conversion to commercial use) are less than 10% of the original cost of the property. Disposing of SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's length purchaser does not trigger recapture if the purchaser continues to use the property all or substantially all (≥90%) for SR&ED.
For corporations and individuals (where no NAL transfer occurred), the Recapture Amount added to Part I tax under subsection 127(27) is the lesser of:

items: Amount 1: The actual SR&ED ITC earned in respect of the particular property; OR

Amount 2: The amount determined by multiplying the historical ITC percentage rate used when earning the credit (35%, 15%, or 20% prior to 2014) by the Proceeds of Disposition (if disposed of to an arm's length person) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's length party).

body.text: Any SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year is added back to the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the current taxation year.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits stack on top of the federal SR&ED program, but constitute "government assistance" under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act—meaning that provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal Section 37 pool and grind the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool on Line 514 of Form T661 (excluding any provincial assistance attributable to pre-December 16, 2024 capital expenditures). Following the enactment of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, provincial responses have split between "Followers" (such as British Columbia) and "Holdouts" or independent reformers (such as Ontario, Quebec, and Alberta).
4.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A, all of which are processed by the CRA alongside the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return and require the corporation to maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario and file a valid federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within the 18-month statutory reporting deadline. Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit. However, because both the ORDTC and the OITC rely on federal qualified expenditures, capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 became eligible for both credits automatically when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, as confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review.

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566): Governed by section 96 (specifically subsections 96(1), 96(3.1), 96(8), 96(12), and 96(14)) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the OITC is an 8% fully refundable tax credit based on the sum of a qualifying CCPC's qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario (including 100% of current expenditures) and any eligible repayments. The maximum annual expenditure limit is $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), which begins to phase out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (eliminated at $800,000) or when prior-year specified capital reaches $25,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000). Claimed by filing Schedule 566 (Ontario Innovation Tax Credit) and entering the credit on Line 468 of Schedule 5 (or waived under subsection 96(14)).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45, Schedule 508): Governed by Part III, Division B, Subdivision c (Sections 38 to 45) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the ORDTC is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years ending on or after June 1, 2016) available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment (with no CCPC requirement and no expenditure cap). Before applying the 3.5% rate on Schedule 508 (Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit), gross eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures must be reduced ("ground") by all government assistance (such as NRC IRAP grants) and by the current-year OITC entitlement calculated on Schedule 566. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years. Claimed on Schedule 508 and entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5, with property recapture under Section 45 calculated on Schedule 508 and entered on Line 277 of Schedule 5.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569): Governed by section 97 (including subsection 97(3)) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the OBRITC provides qualifying corporations with a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI), up to an annual qualified expenditure limit of $20,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), for a maximum annual tax credit of $4,000,000. Claimed by filing Schedule 568 and Schedule 569 and entering the credit on Line 470 of Schedule 5.

body.text: 4.2 Quebec: The CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) and Legacy Credits

Quebec administers its corporate tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec. Following Quebec's 2025–2026 fiscal reform, for all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Quebec government abolished and replaced four former R&D tax credits—(1) the Tax Credit for R&D Wages (formerly Form RD-1029.7 for corporations and Form RD-1029.8.6 for partnership members), (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centres, (3) the Tax Credit for Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Research, and (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium—with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

The CRIC is 100% refundable and provides a 30% enhanced rate on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN and prorated for short taxation years; note that partnership members are ineligible for the 30% rate) and a 20% base rate on all excess eligible expenditures above $1,000,000. The mandatory exclusion threshold is the greater of: (1) $50,000 (prorated by days in the taxation year), or (2) the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold calculated using the basic personal amount applicable to the employees involved.

Crucially, the CRIC covers both R&D carried out in Quebec (where the CRA conducts the scientific review) and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec that continue Quebec R&D—specifically including tests and studies to obtain an initial regulatory registration or certification needed to commercialize a product or process, as well as product design, prototyping, and technological validation (unless the pre-commercialization work is also federal SR&ED, it appears in the Quebec claim only). Eligible CRIC expenditures include 100% of wages paid to employees directly involved in eligible activities (including direct support roles), 50% of arm's length subcontractor payments attributable to Quebec work (requiring the subcontractor's QST number or SIN), payments to eligible research entities, and 100% of acquisitions of new, unused capital property used almost exclusively for eligible activities in Quebec once available for use (excluding land, buildings, and building rights). Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Form RD-222 (Deduction of R&D Expenditures) and Form RD-1029.8.CR with their CO-17 return within 12 months of the CO-17 filing deadline, reporting the R&D portion under Code 112 and the pre-commercialization portion under Code 113.

To illustrate the federal-Quebec coordination, if a corporation incurs $1,200,000 of Quebec R&D salaries and $200,000 to an arm's length Quebec subcontractor (50% = $100,000 eligible), its gross CRIC base is $1,300,000. Subtracting an assumed $100,000 exclusion threshold leaves $1,200,000 of expenditures above the threshold, earning 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000) plus 20% on the remaining $200,000 ($40,000) for a total refundable CRIC of $340,000. If its federal qualified expenditures before the CRIC were $2,000,000, the $340,000 CRIC grinds the federal base to $1,660,000, which earns a 35% federal ITC of $581,000—yielding a combined federal-Quebec refund of $921,000.
4.3 British Columbia

Governed by Part 6 (Sections 98, 99, 100(1), and 102.1 to 102.6) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act and claimed on Form T666 (British Columbia (BC) Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) within 18 months of tax year-end, British Columbia expressly aligned its 10% SR&ED tax credit with the federal Bill C-15 changes for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, while BC Budget 2026 permanently removed the credit expiry date. Under Section 98, qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn a 10% refundable credit (entered on Line 674 of Schedule 5) up to the increased $6,000,000 expenditure limit (phased out over $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital), including restored capital expenditures. Under Section 99, expenditures above the limit and expenditures by other qualifying corporations (including corporate partners) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (entered on Line 659 of Schedule 5), which can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years. Property recapture within 10 years of acquisition under Sections 102.1 to 102.6 is entered on Line 241 of Schedule 5.
4.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act via AT1 Schedule 29 (Form TRA14637, Rev. 2026-06), Alberta published updated guidance on June 30, 2026 confirming that the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) retains its separate provincial structure and did not adopt the federal $6,000,000 limit or federal capital expenditure restoration. Available exclusively to corporations (individuals, partnerships, and trusts are ineligible), the IEG provides an 8% refundable base benefit (Line 110) on eligible Alberta expenditures (Line 031) up to the $4,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit (Line 108, prorated for short years and shared among associated corporations on Page 3 of Schedule 29), plus an additional 12% refundable benefit (Line 112 / Line 125, for a combined 20% refundable rate) on eligible Alberta expenditures exceeding the corporation's "Base Amount" (Line 118)—calculated as the average eligible Alberta expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years ((Line 114 + Line 116) ÷ 2).

For taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, AT1 Schedule 29 (Line 003 / Line 005) requires claimants to start with Line 557 (federal current SR&ED expenditures) of Form T661 rather than Line 559, deducting the federal PPA (Line 007) and adding the Alberta proxy amount (Line 009) and current-year IEG grind (Line 011)—thereby excluding restored federal capital expenditures. The gross IEG (Line 130) is phased out linearly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (Line 126, from Line 690 of federal Schedule T2SCH33) using the factor [$40,000,000 − (Line 126 − $10,000,000)] ÷ $40,000,000 on Line 128. Net IEG after property recapture (Line 132) is entered on Line 134 (transferred to AT1 Page 2, Line 129), and Schedule 29 must be filed within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date (21 months after year-end), contingent on filing federal Form T661 within 18 months of year-end.
4.5 Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes (Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Yukon)

items: Saskatchewan (Schedule 403; Schedule 5 Lines 631 & 645): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the annual qualifying expenditure limit for its 10% refundable R&D tax credit for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (entered on Line 645 of Schedule 5). Expenditures above $2,000,000 and expenditures by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (entered on Line 631 of Schedule 5, carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years), subject to an overall combined annual cap of $1,000,000 in total credits.

Manitoba (Income Tax Act (Manitoba) Subsection 7.3(7); Schedule 380; Schedule 5 Lines 606 & 613): Provides a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible current expenditures, depreciable capital expenditures (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings), and first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE). The 15% credit is 100% refundable when conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute; for all other eligible R&D, 50% is refundable (Line 613 of Schedule 5) and 50% is non-refundable (Line 606 of Schedule 5, carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or renounced under subsection 7.3(7)), filed within 12 months of the T2 filing due date.

body.text: 5. Interaction with Direct Innovation Grants and Government Assistance Stacking
5.1 Statutory Rules on Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d), paragraph 37(1)(d.1), and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act, as explained in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, a claimant must reduce both its Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and its Section 127 qualified SR&ED expenditures by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance (paragraph 12(1)(x)), or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Where assistance is received by one member of a non-arm's length group while other NAL members perform the SR&ED, the group may allocate the assistance reduction using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20).

When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance or contract payments (reported on Line 560 of Form T661), the repayment increases the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and generates an ITC under subsections 127(9) (paragraphs (e.1) and (e.2)), 127(10.7), and 127(10.8) based on the historical ITC rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the pool; however, because repayments are not current-year qualified expenditures, the ITC earned on a repayment of assistance is non-refundable (though eligible for 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward). Furthermore, under subsection 127(26), current expenditures (other than salary or wages) not paid within 180 days of taxation year-end are excluded from qualified expenditures for that year and must be identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline; if not identified on Form T661 within 18 months, they can never be included in qualified expenditures even when paid in a subsequent year.
5.2 National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and ISED Programs

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) supports R&D performed by incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with fewer than 500 full-time equivalent employees through a network of more than 250 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) (slated for integration into the Canada Innovation Corporation [CIC] by 2026–2027). Accessed by contacting NRC IRAP (1-877-994-4727) for ITA triage and collaborative proposal development prior to starting work (retroactive funding is prohibited), NRC IRAP reimburses up to 80% of direct internal technical salary costs and up to 50% of specialized arm's length subcontractor costs, subject to an overall government assistance cap of 75% of total eligible project costs (requiring at least 25% company co-funding). When stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED under the Proxy Method, the IRAP contribution reduces the Section 37 and Section 127 pools as government assistance, but does not reduce the Salary Base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—allowing companies to apply the 35% SR&ED ITC to both the unsubsidized salary portion and the full 55% PPA.

For large-scale innovation projects ($10,000,000 to $250,000,000+), Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and the $5 billion Strategic Response Fund (SRF) enacted under Budget 2025 / Bill C-15, alongside Scale AI (up to 40% reimbursement), the AI Compute Access Fund ($100,000 to $5,000,000), and BOREALIS. As established by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178) and CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527), even non-forgivable repayable government contributions or loans constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) if their terms (such as below-market implicit interest rates) are not strictly commercial—meaning the full principal grinds the claimant's SR&ED ITCs in the year received.
6. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Administration
6.1 Governing Authorities, Prescribed Forms, and the 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline—defined as 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 return is due 6 months after year-end (paragraph 150(1)(a)), a corporation has exactly 18 months after the end of its taxation year to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (while individuals have 12 months after their June 15 T1 due date under subparagraph 150(1)(d)(ii), and partnerships follow Regulations 229(1)–(5)).

Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Act, the CRA cannot by law grant any extension of time to file SR&ED prescribed forms past the 18-month reporting deadline (unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, extending it to the next business day). Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m), if Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 (or required prescribed information) is not filed on time, the expenditures are permanently precluded from being deducted as SR&ED or earning an ITC, and no additional projects or substitute expenditures may be added after the deadline passes. (Note: Use of the Section 37 pool and claim preparer disclosures under subsection 37(11) are not subject to the 18-month deadline).

body.text: 6.2 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026), Review Procedures, and Penalties

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (using Form T1322 via My Business Account, with one-on-one sessions available via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca) for CCPCs, other Canadian corporations, and partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 in good standing with the CRA. Submitted before starting a proposed project or incurring costs, the CRA issues a determination within 8 weeks and can approve projects for up to 3 years. If a pre-approved project's parameters remain consistent when Form T661 is filed, the CRA conducts an expenditure-only review targeting processing within 90 calendar days (alongside its 60-day standard for refundable claims accepted as filed, met 95% of the time in 2025–2026). Claimants may also utilize the CRA's Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC), Pre-Claim Review (PCR), and First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS).

When a filed claim is selected via CORTAX / AIMS for a coordinated review under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (evaluating technical eligibility and issuing an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report with determinations of AW [All Work], SW [Some Work], NW [No Work], UN [Unsubstantiated], or AAF [Accepted As Filed]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (auditing expenditures) conduct a three-step review: Step 1 (initial phone contact and letter with a 30-day information request deadline), Step 2 (virtual or on-site review meeting, interviews, and facility tour—note that covertly recording a meeting requires immediate termination under Chapter 2.10 of the Financial Claim Review Manual), and Step 3 (issuance of a Proposal Package with a 30-day window for written representations).

Before the file closes, disputes follow a three-step informal resolution process under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns: (1) speak with the RTA/FR; (2) escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) / Financial Review Manager (FRM); and (3) submit Form RC532 (Request for an Administrative Review) within the 30-day proposal period to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (427 Laurier Ave W, 13th Floor, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5) for review by the Assistant Director regarding due process and policy consistency. Once a Notice of Assessment/Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 days to file a formal Notice of Objection (paragraph 165(1)(b)), with extensions strictly barred after 1 year and 90 days (subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5)), followed by appeal to the Tax Court of Canada. Finally, under subsection 163(2) (paragraphs 163(2)(a) and (d) and subsection 163(3)), the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy imposes a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of understated Part I tax plus the entire overstated refundable ITC refund claimed, while subsection 239(1.1) imposes criminal fines of 50% to 200% of fraudulent ITC claims.
7. Landmark Judicial Precedents and Case Law Analysis

Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence in the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) establishes the binding legal rules governing technical eligibility, evidentiary proof, statutory filing compliance, and government assistance.
7.1 The Foundational Five-Criteria Test and Its Appellate Endorsement

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC) (May 1, 1998), Judge Donald Bowman established at paragraph 16 the foundational five-criteria approach to SR&ED eligibility: (1) Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (defined as techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field)? (2) Did the claimant formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty (via a five-stage process of observation, clear objective, articulation of uncertainty, hypothesis formulation, and methodical testing)? (3) Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement (noting that the rejection or failure of a hypothesis after testing is itself a technological advancement that reinforces the measure of uncertainty)? and (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (December 11, 2001), the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed the Northwest Hydraulic test for software development, dismissing a claim for a custom International Distributed Lottery System (IDLS) where the challenges were solvable by routine software engineering and the taxpayer failed to retain project documentation or call any developer directly involved in writing the code. Two decades later, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (May 10, 2021, aff'g 2019 TCC 246), the appellant argued that Justice Bowman's third criterion ("scientific method") no longer applied because the statutory text of subsection 248(1) (after moving from Regulation 2900) does not explicitly contain the phrase "scientific method". Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Webb rejected this argument under Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54), holding that Northwest Hydraulic remains binding law repeatedly endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152).
7.2 Evidentiary Standards, System Uncertainty, and Commercial Prototypes

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA Docket A-710-96; December 21, 1998), Justice Robertson reversed the Tax Court and held that: (1) what constitutes SR&ED is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the court, not expert witnesses; (2) missing documentary evidence of "repeatability" is not automatically fatal where other credible evidence exists; and (3) once a trial judge finds as a fact that model testing occurred and a technological advancement was achieved, a prima facie inference arises that systematic research was conducted. Conversely, where testing or contemporaneous records are absent, claims fail: in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (July 7, 2020), Justice Lafleur held that project timelines, hour logs, and source code lacking revision histories or test records do not prove systematic testing; in Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21 (January 31, 2017), Justice Boyle held that hypothesizing natural health product formulations on paper with no testing fails subsection 248(1); in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (January 17, 2017), Justice Sommerfeldt held that post-hoc "Experiment Summary Sheets," routine mechanical engineering, and calling no engineering witnesses failed the taxpayer's burden of proof; and in Murray Arlin Dentistry Professional Corporation v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 133 (April 24, 2012), Justice Woods dismissed a claim where vague oral evidence failed to substantiate a 20% salary allocation or prove work occurred in the taxation years at issue.

In A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 53 (February 28, 2019), Justice Russell denied SR&ED credits for attempting to fix purchased Italian Tacchi lathes, but allowed 100% of 2007 ITCs (and 1/3 of 2008 ITCs) for building custom 80-ton Matteo lathes due to "system uncertainty", and allowed 100% of 2006–2008 ITCs for an abandoned double-wheel roll grinding machine because technological advancement occurs even in defeat. Similarly, in 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376 (October 25, 2012), Justice Hogan allowed $387,553 in expenditures based on "system uncertainty", shifted unpaid 2007 expenses to 2008 under subsection 127(26), and held that the taxpayer's Informal Procedure election capped additional refundable ITC relief at $12,000 under section 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act (following Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc. v. The Queen, 2009 FCA 302). In 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77 (March 31, 2015), Justice D'Auray held that the prior commercial release of 200 miniature wireless printers in 2008 did not bar 2009–2010 SR&ED claims when unforeseen system-level uncertainties (paper curling and battery drain) forced a market recall. And in Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, 94 DTC 1725 (TCC; August 15, 1994), Judge McArthur held that the "all or substantially all" (ASA) test for a prototype green-sand refiner is evaluated during active SR&ED prosecution, not with hindsight when the successful prototype continues in commercial production.
7.3 Strict Statutory Filing, Government Assistance, Discovery, and Criminal Fraud

The Federal Court of Appeal strictly enforces the 18-month prescribed form and information requirements: in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301 (November 28, 2016, aff'g 2015 TCC 211), Justice Nadon held that filing Form T661 on time did not save the taxpayer's ITC when Schedule T2SCH31 was filed six weeks past the 18-month deadline under paragraph 127(9)(m), ruling that Section 32 of the Interpretation Act cannot excuse an unfiled prescribed form; in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57 (March 21, 2018, aff'g 2017 TCC 9), Justice Woods held that leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 was fatal under subsections 37(11) and 37(12) even though the CRA possessed the project details from a related company and prior filings; in 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 511 (October 14, 2009), Justice Bowie dismissed a claim where the technical report was faxed 12 days after the subsection 37(11) deadline; and in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146 (October 14, 2025), Justice Ouimet confirmed that CRA BCCS mailing records trigger irrebuttable deemed receipt under subsections 244(14)–(15) and 248(7), barring any objection extension past 1 year and 90 days under subsection 166.2(5).

Finally, on government assistance, discovery, and fraud: in CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (October 19, 2022, aff'g 2021 TCC 57) and The Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc., 96 DTC 6527 (FCA; September 19, 1996), the Federal Court of Appeal held that non-forgivable government R&D loans and contributions whose terms are not strictly commercial ("ordinary business agreements") constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x) that grinds SR&ED ITCs and enters taxable income; in Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58 (February 20, 2014), Justice D'Arcy enjoined the CRA from using pre-trial discovery documents to issue collateral reassessments in violation of the implied undertaking rule (Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8; Section 241 of the Act does not displace discovery rules) and awarded $25,000 in costs; and in R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora Inc., Maged Elhami, and Shady Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684 (March 27, 2017), the Court of Quebec imposed criminal fines of $1,324,294 (100% of the fraudulent ITC claimed) against each of the three co-defendants under subsection 239(1.1) for fabricating $4,500,000 in contractor invoices, even though the CRA rejected the claim and disbursed $0.

Affirmed Northwest Hydraulic for software claims; complex custom software built via routine engineering is ineligible; failure to call first-hand developers is fatal.
